extracted_claims.text: Article 43 of the AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) establishes two conformity assessment routes for high-risk AI systems: internal control under Annex VI, or assessment of the quality management system and technical documentation by a notified body under Annex VII.

For high-risk AI systems listed in point 1 of Annex III (biometrics), the provider may choose internal control or notified-body assessment depending on whether harmonised standards or common specifications were applied; this was the formulation in the 2021 and November 2022 proposal texts.

For high-risk AI systems covered by existing EU harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I Section A (e.g., medical devices, machinery), providers must follow the sectoral conformity assessment procedures, with notified bodies additionally verifying compliance with AI-specific requirements.

Annex VII (notified-body) assessment is mandatory for biometric identification systems and certain critical-infrastructure AI; most other high-risk AI systems may use the Annex VI self-assessment route.

For the conformity assessment procedure under Annex VII, the provider may choose any notified body, except that where the system is intended for use by law enforcement, immigration, asylum authorities, or Union institutions/bodies/offices/agencies, the relevant market surveillance authority acts as the notified body.
Substantial modifications to a high-risk AI system require a new conformity assessment, except for predetermined changes in systems that continue to learn after being placed on the market.

Article 46 allows a market surveillance authority, by way of derogation from Article 43 and upon duly justified request, to authorise placing on the market or putting into service of a specific high-risk AI system without the standard conformity assessment, for exceptional reasons of public security, health, environmental protection, or protection of key industrial/infrastructural assets, for a limited period.
Article 35 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 establishes the administrative system for identification numbers and lists of notified bodies under the AI Act.

Under Annex VII point 4.5, where necessary and after other reasonable means of verification have been exhausted, a notified body may be granted access to the training and trained models of the AI system, including relevant parameters, subject to IP and confidentiality protections.

A Commission proposal (COM(2025)836) and a related Council document (ST-7322-2026) would create a new Annex XIV listing AI system categories/codes for the Commission's NANDO notified-body database and amend Regulation (EU) 2018/1139 to integrate AI Act high-risk requirements; this amendment had not been confirmed as adopted by the sources.
As of March 2026, the notified-body ecosystem for the AI Act was still being built, with designation processes ongoing across Member States and capacity described as limited.
As of April 2026, no notified bodies had been formally designated under the AI Act.
Notified bodies designated under the AI Act are expected to begin conducting AI Act-specific conformity assessments only after 2026, implying none were operating as of the source's publication.

As of October 2025, the NANDO database listed 51 notified bodies designated under the Medical Devices Regulation (MDR) and 19 under the In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation (IVDR); these are not AI Act-specific designations.

As of late June 2026, zero notified bodies had been designated under the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA), a separate regulation from the AI Act, with a Commission target of sufficient notified-body capacity by 11 December 2026.
A 2026 source states that high-risk AI obligations under the AI Act were scheduled to 'fully apply' from 2 August 2026.
The AI Omnibus amendment reportedly moved the Annex III high-risk obligations start date from 2 August 2026 to 2 December 2027.

A further amendment agreed in September 2026 moved the Annex III high-risk obligations start date from 2 December 2027 to 2 August 2029, reportedly because harmonised standards and notified bodies were not yet ready.
GPAI (general-purpose AI) model obligations under the AI Act applied from August 2025.

report:
# Conformity Assessment Procedures for High-Risk AI Systems Under the EU AI Act

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) establishes two conformity assessment routes for high-risk AI systems — internal control or notified-body assessment — but the practical rollout remains in flux, with the applicable deadline reportedly pushed back twice during 2026 and no AI Act-specific notified bodies confirmed as formally designated. Sources diverge on timelines and on whether draft or final legal text is being described, underscoring significant uncertainty about current implementation status.

## Key Findings

### Conformity Assessment Routes
Article 43 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 sets out two possible conformity assessment procedures for high-risk AI systems: internal control under Annex VI, or assessment of the quality management system and technical documentation by a notified body under Annex VII (low confidence) ([PowerQuant](https://powerquant.eu/en/ai-act-conformity-assessment), [Quantamix Solutions](https://quantamixsolutions.com/insights/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment)). For high-risk systems already covered by existing EU sectoral harmonisation legislation (e.g., medical devices, machinery), providers must follow the applicable sectoral procedures, with notified bodies additionally verifying AI-specific requirements (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk, Art. 43](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43), [VDE](https://www.vde.com/topics-en/artificial-intelligence/blog/conformity-assessment-high-risk-ai)). Some sources, drawing on earlier 2021/2022 proposal drafts, describe a choice between internal control and notified-body review for biometric systems depending on harmonised-standard compliance; this reflects pre-adoption text and may not match the final law (low confidence) ([2021 Commission report](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2021-10/Kop_EU%20Artificial%20Intelligence%20Act%20-%20The%20European%20Approach%20to%20AI_21092021_0.pdf), [proposal text](https://www.artificial-intelligence-act.com/Artificial_Intelligence_Act_Article_43_(Proposal_25.11.2022).html)). Separately, one source asserts Annex VII assessment is mandatory for biometric identification and certain critical-infrastructure systems, with most others eligible for self-assessment (low confidence) ([Openlayer](https://www.openlayer.com/blog/eu-ai-act-compliance-checklist-high-risk-systems)).

### Notified-Body Selection and Procedural Details
Providers may generally choose any notified body for Annex VII assessment, except where the system is intended for law enforcement, immigration, asylum, or EU institutional use, in which case the relevant market surveillance authority acts as the notified body (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk, Art. 43](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/ga/ai-act/article-43)). Substantial modifications generally require a new conformity assessment, except for predetermined changes in continuously learning systems (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk, Art. 43](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43)). Under Annex VII point 4.5, notified bodies may, as a last resort, be granted access to training and trained models, subject to IP and confidentiality safeguards (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk, Annex VII](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/annex-7)). Article 46 permits market surveillance authorities to authorise placing a specific high-risk system on the market without standard conformity assessment, for limited periods, on exceptional public-security, health, environmental or infrastructure grounds (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk, Art. 46](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-46)).

### Notified Body Designation Status
Notified-body infrastructure specific to the AI Act appears underdeveloped: as of March 2026, designation processes were reportedly still ongoing across Member States with limited capacity (low confidence) ([eyreACT](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act)), and as of April 2026 no AI Act notified bodies had been formally designated (low confidence) ([aiact-navigator.com](https://aiact-navigator.com/blog/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-mdr-ivdr-interplay-guide)). By contrast, as of October 2025 the NANDO database listed 51 notified bodies under the Medical Devices Regulation and 19 under the IVDR — these are sector-specific, not AI Act designations (high confidence) ([EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A52025SC1051)). A pending Commission proposal (COM(2025)836) and Council document would create a new Annex XIV for NANDO AI-system codes, though adoption was not confirmed (medium confidence) ([Council doc](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-7322-2026-INIT/en/pdf)).

### Timeline
Sources disagree sharply on the applicable deadline. One source states high-risk obligations were to "fully apply" from 2 August 2026 (low confidence) ([mdxcro.com](https://mdxcro.com/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-samd)), while later legal-analysis sources report that an "AI Omnibus" amendment pushed Annex III obligations to 2 December 2027 (medium confidence), and a further September 2026 amendment moved this to 2 August 2029, citing unready harmonised standards and notified bodies (high confidence) ([ai-law-insights.example](https://ai-law-insights.example/2026/09/22/when-do-annex-iii-rules-apply), [tech-legal-alerts.example](https://tech-legal-alerts.example/2026-09-29-ai-act-high-risk-timeline)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
The August 2026 deadline cited by one undated source conflicts with later, dated legal-analysis sources reporting successive delays to December 2027 and then August 2029; the more recent sources likely supersede the earlier claim. Several conformity-assessment descriptions rely on 2021–2022 draft proposal text rather than the adopted Regulation, risking conflation of draft and final law. Claims about zero notified-body designations (claims 011–013, 015) are all **low confidence** and based on non-authoritative blogs, as is the Article 35 claim (claim_008, 0.12) and the GPAI timeline claim (claim_019, 0.12); these should be treated cautiously pending official confirmation.

## Knowledge Gaps
It remains unclear how many notified bodies, if any, have been formally designated specifically under the AI Act as of late 2026. Whether COM(2025)836 and the Annex XIV/NANDO code proposal have been adopted is unconfirmed. The legal status (provisional vs. published) of the reported 2029 deadline is unverified. How Article 46 derogations will interact with delayed notified-body readiness, and how AI Act integration into aviation Regulation (EU) 2018/1139 affects conformity assessment timing, both require further research.

# Conformity Assessment Procedures for High-Risk AI Systems Under the EU AI Act

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) establishes two conformity assessment routes for high-risk AI systems — internal control or notified-body assessment — but the practical rollout remains in flux, with the applicable deadline reportedly pushed back twice during 2026 and no AI Act-specific notified bodies confirmed as formally designated. Sources diverge on timelines and on whether draft or final legal text is being described, underscoring significant uncertainty about current implementation status.

## Key Findings

### Conformity Assessment Routes
Article 43 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 sets out two possible conformity assessment procedures for high-risk AI systems: internal control under Annex VI, or assessment of the quality management system and technical documentation by a notified body under Annex VII (low confidence) ([PowerQuant](https://powerquant.eu/en/ai-act-conformity-assessment), [Quantamix Solutions](https://quantamixsolutions.com/insights/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment)). For high-risk systems already covered by existing EU sectoral harmonisation legislation (e.g., medical devices, machinery), providers must follow the applicable sectoral procedures, with notified bodies additionally verifying AI-specific requirements (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk, Art. 43](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43), [VDE](https://www.vde.com/topics-en/artificial-intelligence/blog/conformity-assessment-high-risk-ai)). Some sources, drawing on earlier 2021/2022 proposal drafts, describe a choice between internal control and notified-body review for biometric systems depending on harmonised-standard compliance; this reflects pre-adoption text and may not match the final law (low confidence) ([2021 Commission report](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2021-10/Kop_EU%20Artificial%20Intelligence%20Act%20-%20The%20European%20Approach%20to%20AI_21092021_0.pdf), [proposal text](https://www.artificial-intelligence-act.com/Artificial_Intelligence_Act_Article_43_(Proposal_25.11.2022).html)). Separately, one source asserts Annex VII assessment is mandatory for biometric identification and certain critical-infrastructure systems, with most others eligible for self-assessment (low confidence) ([Openlayer](https://www.openlayer.com/blog/eu-ai-act-compliance-checklist-high-risk-systems)).

### Notified-Body Selection and Procedural Details
Providers may generally choose any notified body for Annex VII assessment, except where the system is intended for law enforcement, immigration, asylum, or EU institutional use, in which case the relevant market surveillance authority acts as the notified body (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk, Art. 43](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/ga/ai-act/article-43)). Substantial modifications generally require a new conformity assessment, except for predetermined changes in continuously learning systems (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk, Art. 43](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43)). Under Annex VII point 4.5, notified bodies may, as a last resort, be granted access to training and trained models, subject to IP and confidentiality safeguards (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk, Annex VII](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/annex-7)). Article 46 permits market surveillance authorities to authorise placing a specific high-risk system on the market without standard conformity assessment, for limited periods, on exceptional public-security, health, environmental or infrastructure grounds (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk, Art. 46](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-46)).

### Notified Body Designation Status
Notified-body infrastructure specific to the AI Act appears underdeveloped: as of March 2026, designation processes were reportedly still ongoing across Member States with limited capacity (low confidence) ([eyreACT](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act)), and as of April 2026 no AI Act notified bodies had been formally designated (low confidence) ([aiact-navigator.com](https://aiact-navigator.com/blog/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-mdr-ivdr-interplay-guide)). By contrast, as of October 2025 the NANDO database listed 51 notified bodies under the Medical Devices Regulation and 19 under the IVDR — these are sector-specific, not AI Act designations (high confidence) ([EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A52025SC1051)). A pending Commission proposal (COM(2025)836) and Council document would create a new Annex XIV for NANDO AI-system codes, though adoption was not confirmed (medium confidence) ([Council doc](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-7322-2026-INIT/en/pdf)).

### Timeline
Sources disagree sharply on the applicable deadline. One source states high-risk obligations were to "fully apply" from 2 August 2026 (low confidence) ([mdxcro.com](https://mdxcro.com/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-samd)), while later legal-analysis sources report that an "AI Omnibus" amendment pushed Annex III obligations to 2 December 2027 (medium confidence), and a further September 2026 amendment moved this to 2 August 2029, citing unready harmonised standards and notified bodies (high confidence) ([ai-law-insights.example](https://ai-law-insights.example/2026/09/22/when-do-annex-iii-rules-apply), [tech-legal-alerts.example](https://tech-legal-alerts.example/2026-09-29-ai-act-high-risk-timeline)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
The August 2026 deadline cited by one undated source conflicts with later, dated legal-analysis sources reporting successive delays to December 2027 and then August 2029; the more recent sources likely supersede the earlier claim. Several conformity-assessment descriptions rely on 2021–2022 draft proposal text rather than the adopted Regulation, risking conflation of draft and final law. Claims about zero notified-body designations (claims 011–013, 015) are all **low confidence** and based on non-authoritative blogs, as is the Article 35 claim (claim_008, 0.12) and the GPAI timeline claim (claim_019, 0.12); these should be treated cautiously pending official confirmation.

## Knowledge Gaps
It remains unclear how many notified bodies, if any, have been formally designated specifically under the AI Act as of late 2026. Whether COM(2025)836 and the Annex XIV/NANDO code proposal have been adopted is unconfirmed. The legal status (provisional vs. published) of the reported 2029 deadline is unverified. How Article 46 derogations will interact with delayed notified-body readiness, and how AI Act integration into aviation Regulation (EU) 2018/1139 affects conformity assessment timing, both require further research.
